text:
I had ~500 user IDs to fetch, so I mapped each one to a fetch call and wrapped it in Promise.all. It flew through my 5-item test.

Against the real list, the API started returning 429 Too Many Requests almost instantly. My "map everything" approach had fired 500 requests at once.

The fix isn't going sequential. One request at a time turned a 4-second job into a 3-minute crawl and wasted all the concurrency the API actually allowed.

The answer is bounded concurrency: run in parallel, but never more than N tasks at once.

Two ways to build it:

Chunking - slice the array into batches of N, await Promise.all on each batch. Simple and correct. The catch: one slow task stalls its whole batch, so finished slots sit idle.

Worker pool - start N tasks, and the moment any one finishes, that slot grabs the next item. You stay pinned at N in flight until the work runs out. Two details make it work: write each result by its index (so order survives out-of-order completion), and keep a settled flag so the first error rejects everything and no new tasks start.

Use chunking when tasks take similar time. Use a worker pool when durations vary, which for network calls they always do.

I wrote up the full build with a runnable test suite:

https://blog.sandeepallala.com/blog/implementing-map-async-limit-javascript-utility-function
